uncited: The method minimizes the discrepancy between the forward-projected volume and the ground-truth projection data.
- **Input Volume ($x$):** The predicted volumetric representation (e.g., density field, SDF, or radiance field) parameterized by a neural network or grid.
- **Input Projections ($y$):** The measured projection data (e.g., sinogram pixels, image pixels).
- **Forward Projection Operator ($A$):** A differentiable operator that simulates the acquisition process (e.g., ray marching for optical views, line integrals for X-rays).
**Forward Pass:** Compute the predicted volume $x$ using the model.
- For optical views, this involves sampling the volume along camera rays and compositing colors/opacities using the standard emission-absorption model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
Non-differentiable approximations (e.g., hard thresholding) will break the optimization.
- **Scale Ambiguity:** In single-view scenarios, depth scale ambiguity may require additional constraints (e.g., Monocular Depth Consistency Loss) [4668-monocular-depth-consistency-loss.md].
Regularizing $b$ with MSE or cosine similarity yields no significant performance impact.
- **Time Complexity:** Depends on the forward projection operator.
For ray marching, it is $O(N_{rays} \cdot N_{samples})$.
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing intermediate states for backpropagation through the forward projector.
Adjoint methods or analytic inversion can reduce this to $O(N_{rays})$ [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
The method leverages the differentiability of the forward rendering operator to propagate gradients from the projection space to the volume space [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
